name: Number System
intro: **Prime-factorise first, ask the question second.** Factor counts, HCF, LCM, perfect-power conditions and trailing zeroes all fall straight out of the factorisation (§3).
For remainders, look for the small power that is ≡ 1 or ≡ −1. That collapses the exponent immediately (§6).

qs.q: Find the number of factors of 720.
qs.h: §3 — factorise, then multiply (exponent + 1) across the primes.

qs.q: The number of even factors of 360 is
qs.h: §3 — an even factor must take at least one 2, so the exponent of 2 has 3 choices, not 4.

qs.q: Find the sum of all factors of 200.
qs.h: §3 — the sum of factors is the product of the geometric sums over each prime.

qs.q: The largest 3-digit number divisible by both 8 and 12 is
qs.h: §4 — divisible by both means divisible by their LCM, which is 24, not 96.

qs.q: How many trailing zeroes does 100! have?
qs.h: §12 — count the 5s, not the 2s, and don't forget that 25, 50, 75 and 100 each contribute an extra one.

qs.q: The number of factors of 1800 that are perfect squares is
qs.h: §10 — a perfect-square factor needs every exponent even, so count the even choices for each prime.

qs.q: Find the HCF of 108 and 144.
qs.h: §4 — take the lowest power of each shared prime.

qs.q: The LCM of two numbers is 495 and their HCF is 5. If their sum is 100, the numbers are
qs.h: §4 — the product of the numbers is HCF × LCM. With the sum known, they are the roots of a quadratic.
qs.s: Product = 5 × 495 = 2475 with sum 100 ⟹ x² − 100x + 2475 = 0 ⟹ x = 45 and 55. (Check: HCF 5, LCM 495 ✓ — the other options fail the HCF test.)

qs.q: Find the greatest number that divides 43, 91 and 183 leaving the same remainder in each case.
qs.h: §4 — if the remainder is equal but unknown, it cancels in the differences. Take the HCF of the differences.
qs.s: Differences 48, 92 and 140 ⟹ HCF = 4. (Each of 43, 91, 183 leaves remainder 3 on division by 4 ✓)

qs.q: The least number which, when divided by 5, 6, 7 and 8, leaves remainder 3 in each case is
qs.h: §4 — a common remainder means LCM + remainder.

qs.q: Three bells toll at intervals of 9, 12 and 15 minutes. If they toll together at 9:00 a.m., after how many minutes do they next toll together?
qs.h: §4 — simultaneous events recur at the LCM of the intervals.

qs.q: The HCF of two numbers is 12 and their LCM is 336. If one number is 84, the other is
qs.h: §4 — HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers.

qs.q: Find the unit digit of 7¹⁰⁵.
qs.h: §5 — 7 has a cycle of 4: 7, 9, 3, 1. Reduce the exponent modulo 4.
qs.s: 105 mod 4 = 1 ⟹ the first entry of the cycle ⟹ unit digit 7.

qs.q: The unit digit of 2⁶⁴ is
qs.h: §5 — cycle 2, 4, 8, 6. A remainder of 0 means the last entry, not the first.
qs.s: 64 mod 4 = 0 ⟹ the fourth entry ⟹ unit digit 6.

qs.q: Find the unit digit of 13⁴⁷ × 17²³.
qs.h: §5 — only the unit digits 3 and 7 matter; handle each cycle separately, then multiply.

qs.q: The unit digit of 1! + 2! + 3! + … + 100! is
qs.h: §12 — every factorial from 5! onward ends in 0, so only four terms matter.

qs.q: Find the unit digit of 4³⁷³.
qs.h: §5 — 4 has a cycle of length 2: odd powers end in 4, even powers in 6.

qs.q: Find the remainder when 2⁵¹ is divided by 7.
qs.h: §6 — hunt for the small power ≡ 1. Here 2³ = 8 ≡ 1 (mod 7).

qs.q: The remainder when 15²³ is divided by 16 is
qs.h: §6 — write 15 as −1 modulo 16. An odd power keeps the sign.

qs.q: Find the remainder when 7¹⁰⁰ is divided by 100.
The remainder when 16! is divided by 17 is
qs.h: §6 — Wilson's theorem: (p − 1)! ≡ −1 (mod p) for a prime p.
qs.s: 17 is prime ⟹ 16! ≡ −1 ≡ 16 (mod 17). (A remainder can never equal the divisor, which rules out option (d) instantly.)

qs.q: A number divided by 296 leaves remainder 75. What remainder does it leave when divided by 37?
qs.h: §6 — 296 is a multiple of 37, so that part vanishes and only the remainder needs reducing.

qs.q: The remainder when 3⁵⁷ is divided by 8 is
qs.h: §6 — 3² = 9 ≡ 1 (mod 8), so only the parity of the exponent matters.

sets.name: Perfect squares, cubes and least multipliers

qs.q: Find the least positive integer n such that 1176n is a perfect square.
qs.h: §10 — factorise, then supply exactly what is missing to make every exponent even.
qs.s: 1176 = 2³ × 3 × 7². The 2 and the 3 have odd exponents ⟹ n = 2 × 3 = 6. (1176 × 6 = 7056 = 84² ✓)

qs.q: The least number by which 8232 must be divided to give a perfect cube is
qs.h: §10 — for a cube, every exponent must be a multiple of 3. Here you remove rather than add.

qs.q: How many perfect squares lie strictly between 100 and 1000?
qs.h: §10 — find the first and last integer whose square lies in range, then count inclusively.

qs.q: The smallest number that must be added to 1780 to make it a perfect square is
qs.h: §10 — locate the nearest squares on either side: 42² and 43².

qs.q: Find the smallest positive integer by which 2925 must be multiplied to become a perfect square.
qs.h: §10 — factorise and look for the lone prime.

qs.q: How many solutions in positive integers does 3x + 5y = 100 have?
qs.h: §11 — reduce modulo the smaller coefficient to pin down y, then step by 3.
qs.s: 5y ≡ 100 (mod 3) ⟹ 2y ≡ 1 ⟹ y ≡ 2 (mod 3) ⟹ y = 2, 5, 8, 11, 14, 17 ⟹ 6 solutions. (y = 20 gives x = 0, which is not positive.)

qs.q: The number of non-negative integer solutions of 2x + 3y = 30 is
qs.h: §11 — 3y must be even, so y must be even. Note that here 0 is allowed.

qs.q: If x and y are positive integers satisfying 7x + 11y = 100, find x + y.
qs.h: §11 — reduce modulo 7 to fix y, then check that only one value stays in range.
qs.s: 4y ≡ 2 (mod 7) ⟹ y ≡ 4 (mod 7). Only y = 4 keeps 11y below 100 ⟹ x = 8 ⟹ x + y = 12.

qs.q: The number of solutions of x + y + z = 10 in positive integers is
qs.h: §11 — stars and bars: C(n − 1, r − 1) for positive solutions.
qs.s: C(9, 2) = 36. (66 = C(12, 2) is the non-negative count — the planted decoy.)

qs.q: Pens cost ₹7 each and notebooks ₹9 each. A man spends exactly ₹62 and buys at least one of each. Find the number of notebooks.
qs.h: §11 — reduce modulo 7 to fix the number of notebooks; the range does the rest.
qs.s: 2y ≡ 6 (mod 7) ⟹ y ≡ 3 (mod 7). y = 10 already exceeds ₹62 ⟹ y = 3 notebooks (and 5 pens: 35 + 27 = 62 ✓).

qs.q: Find the number of factors of 2520.
qs.h: Factorise first.

qs.q: The unit digit of 3²⁰²⁰ is
qs.h: Cycle of 4; a remainder of 0 points to the last entry.

qs.q: Find the remainder when 5⁹⁹ is divided by 13.
The HCF of 391, 425 and 527 is
qs.h: All three are products of a common two-digit prime.

qs.q: How many zeroes are at the end of 50!?
qs.h: Count the 5s.

qs.q: The least number which when divided by 12, 15 and 20 leaves remainders 5, 8 and 13 respectively is
qs.h: Each remainder falls short of its divisor by the same amount.

qs.q: Find the smallest positive integer n such that 720n is a perfect cube.
qs.h: Bring every exponent up to the next multiple of 3.

qs.q: The number of even factors of 2⁴ × 3³ × 5² is
qs.h: The exponent of 2 must be at least 1.

qs.q: The sum of two numbers is 528 and their HCF is 33. How many such pairs of numbers exist?
qs.h: Write them as 33a and 33b with a and b coprime.

qs.q: The remainder when 32^(32^32) is divided by 7 is
qs.h: Reduce the base mod 7 first, then reduce the tower exponent mod the cycle length.

audit: counting factors without first prime-factorising, or forgetting the constraint that makes a factor even or square (§3, §10)
using the product instead of the LCM, or the wrong direction of HCF × LCM = product (§4)
A5, M5
counting 2s instead of 5s, or missing the second-order terms ⌊n/25⌋
B3
not realising an unknown common remainder cancels in the differences
reading a remainder of 0 as the first entry of the cycle rather than the last (§5)
C4
summing all 100 factorials instead of stopping at 4!
brute-forcing the exponent instead of finding the small power ≡ 1 (§6)
D2
not using the ≡ −1 shortcut, which handles odd exponents in one line
D5
reducing modulo the wrong number — 296 is already a multiple of 37
adding when the question says divide, or stopping before every exponent is fixed (§10)
F1, F2
confusing positive with non-negative solutions — the endpoints are exactly what differ (§11)
F4
using C(n + r − 1, r − 1) where positive solutions need C(n − 1, r − 1)
M9
forgetting the coprimality condition on the co-factors
